## Choose **one** prompt to answer

## Response

<!-- RESPONSE-START -->
Self-selection bias is one form of bias that stands out to me the most, and it can have a pretty big impact on the studies of online news consumption. For example, imagine if a survey  asks people to share what kinds of news websites they visit. The people who chose to respond are more than likely the ones who already care about news or are confident in their media habits. But those who consume less news or feel guilty about spending more time on entertainment sites rather than news sites, are less likely to participate in the survey. As a result, this can skew the sample toward more heavier and more meticulous news consumers, creating an impressions that the public is more engaged with the news than they actually are.  This can be really tricky in digital spaces, where participation is often voluntary. A similar issue shows up in streaming habits. If a researcher were to ask people to report what they watch, those who see their viewing choices as maybe "smarter" or "more socially acceptable" may respond quicker. This kind of "selective participation" distorts the data, painting a picture that doesn't fully represent the broader population. To address this bias, researchers can combine self-reported data with behavioral data, like anonymous logs from different streaming platforms and the analytics from the news sights. It is important that they acknowledge the limitations of the study at the beginning, such as saying the data reflecting the choices of those who chose to opt in to the survey. The most important thing they can do is design studies that can reach a wider pool of participants, maybe by offering incentives or recruiting outside of the usual online channels. By being transparent about self-selection bias and trying to find ways to balance it, researchers can provide a more realistic picture of how people actually consume digital media. 
<!-- RESPONSE-END -->

## Word Count & Range Check

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
get_response_text <- function() {
  f <- knitr::current_input()
  if (is.null(f) || !file.exists(f)) return("")
  x <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
  # Find the lines that EXACTLY match the start/end markers
  s <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-START -->$", x)
  e <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-END -->$", x)
  if (length(s) != 1 || length(e) != 1 || e <= s) return("")
  paste(x[(s + 1L):(e - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
}
count_words <- function(txt) {
  # Remove code blocks and inline code before counting
  txt <- gsub("```[\\s\\S]*?```", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub("`[^`]*`", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Keep letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes
  txt <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}\\s'-]", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Split by whitespace and count non-empty words
  words <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  length(words)
}
txt <- get_response_text()
n <- count_words(txt)
minw <- as.integer(params$word_min)
maxw <- as.integer(params$word_max)
in_range <- n >= minw && n <= maxw
cat(sprintf("**Word count:** %d  \n", n))
cat(sprintf("**Required range (%s):** %d–%d words  \n",
            toupper(params$course), minw, maxw))
cat(if (in_range) "**Status:** ✅ In range\n" else "**Status:** ❌ Out of range\n")
```
